expectations.text: The ROAS-drop answer opens by scoping the comparison window, noting a drop measured over a week or less is often noise
expectations.evidence: "Three weeks is enough to rule out noise, but I'd still confirm this against the same three weeks last month and against a longer trailing average"

expectations.text: The ROAS-drop diagnostic is presented as an ordered sequence, not an unordered list of possibilities
expectations.evidence: "I'd check these in order of hit-rate per minute spent checking, not just likelihood" followed by numbered steps 1-5

expectations.text: Creative health comes first, citing fatigue as the cause roughly 60-70% of the time, checked via frequency and the age of the top-spending creatives
expectations.evidence: "Creative health (check first — causes ~60-70% of drops)... I'd pull frequency and the age of the top-spending ads."

expectations.text: Audience saturation comes second, identified by rising CPM against flat reach
expectations.evidence: "Audience saturation... Rising CPMs against flat or shrinking reach on the core segments."

expectations.text: Site-side conversion comes third: landing page, offer, price, or checkout changes the ad account cannot fix
expectations.evidence: "Did anything change on the landing page, offer, subscription pricing, or checkout... The ad account can't fix a site problem"

expectations.text: Attribution or tracking accuracy comes last, with the note that a reporting artefact is not a performance drop
expectations.evidence: Transcript places attribution last ("I'd check this last precisely because it's the one people jump to first and it's rarely the answer") but never states the concept that a reporting artefact is not a genuine performance drop.

expectations.text: States the ordering's rationale: hit rate per minute of checking, not likelihood alone (in-account checks take minutes; site-side is a cross-team ask)
expectations.evidence: "Creative and audience are visible in the account in minutes; site-side and attribution mean pulling in other teams, so I check them last"

expectations.text: Closes the diagnosis with the business metric that decides it: blended MER or contribution, not the platform dashboard alone
expectations.evidence: "I'd report it against blended MER or contribution margin, not just platform ROAS"

expectations.text: The p=0.08 answer refuses the binary significant-or-not framing and answers with a decision frame
expectations.evidence: "Don't answer 'significant' or 'not significant' — that's the trap. Answer with a decision frame."

expectations.text: The decision frame weighs the cost of being wrong in each direction: cheap-to-keep with small downside means ship and keep measuring, expensive or irreversible means extend the test
expectations.evidence: "If this was a creative or copy variant — cheap to keep running... I'd ship it" vs "If it's something expensive or hard to reverse... I'd extend the test"

expectations.text: Notes that naming the threshold as something that should have been agreed before the test reads as senior
expectations.evidence: "naming 'the threshold should have been set before the test' is the tell interviewers listen for"

expectations.text: The budget-doubling answer names audience saturation or diminishing marginal returns: the algorithm reaches beyond the efficient core of the audience to spend the larger budget
expectations.evidence: "That's audience saturation — diminishing marginal returns... it reaches past the efficient core into colder, more competitive, more expensive placements"

expectations.text: Connects the budget-doubling mechanics to the rising-CPM signal or identifies it as the saturation diagnosis in disguise
expectations.evidence: "CPM goes up because you're now bidding against more advertisers for scarcer attention within that audience"
